Benjamin Wolstein  

Kvarnes, M.D., Robert G. and Gloria H. Parloff (eds.), et al., A Harry Stack Sullivan Case Seminar: Treatment of a Young Male Schizophrenic. New York, Norton, 1976.

THIS BOOK, THE PRESENTATION of a case seminar, is genuine, vintage Sullivan, recorded live and offered in transcript form with later reflective commentary. It joins the growing body of posthumous work that his colleagues, students, and various coworkers are wisely deciding to organize, edit, and commit to print for enduring reference. These posthumous publications consist largely of transcripts of his discussions of theoretical concepts and therapeutic procedures, and of collections of his papers on a wide variety of topics in psychiatry, social policy and cultural values, and international relations. And now, in this volume under comment, the theme is his conduct of a seminar on the ongoing treatment of a young male schizophrenic.

The editors, Robert G. Kvarnes, M.D., and Gloria Parloff, and the commentators, John C. Dillingham, Stanley Jacobson, Ed.D., Robert G. Kvarnes, M.D., and Irving M. Rykoff, M.D., are to be congratulated for holding fast to their labor of love over the years until it could appear in hard cover, not only for their dedicated editing of the original 1946-1947 seminar led by Sullivan, and attended by a number of serious and penetrating participants, but also for their thoughtful 1971-1972 commentary on each of the five meetings. They seek to place the Sullivan legacy into historical focus from the perspective of the post-Sullivanian and even neo-Sullivanian present.

Maurice Green  

Leston Havens: Participant Observation New York: Jason Aronson 1976.

LESTON HAVENS, IN THE CONSERVATIVE sanctuary of Boston psychoanalysis and Harvard Medical School, has rediscovered Harry Stack Sullivan, and with great skill and clarity has accomplished the task, long spoken of, but heretofore never completed, of explicating Sullivan for the sophisticated, dynamic psychotherapist.

In the first chapter, practically entitled Sullivan's Fine Disregard he confronts the reader immediately with the almost awesome respect and painstaking regard Sullivan had for the patient's self esteem, while at the same time (and in the service of this painstaking care) Sullivan was sarcastic, mocking and offhand. He shows how Sullivan daringly operates on his inferences of what sort of fantastic projection of interpersonal relations the patient is experiencing, imagining in himself, the subjective reality of the patient's world. He precisely expresses himself in attitude, gesture and words to counter the patient's projection and expected behavior of the other. In this respect, Sullivan could be strategic and manipulative, lulling the patient into going out much farther than originally intended, so that the patient is, as it were, hoisted in his own petard. Sullivan is presented as the conductor orchestrating himself and the patient with the imaginary significant others, increasing and decreasing the volume of anxiety to a code of relief, and enhanced well-being for the patient.

What we read here reflects Havens' fine sense of humor and dramatic insight into the heart of Sullivan's innovations: The Other People in the Room; Managing Conflict; Two Illustrations; An Interview; The Interpersonal Perspective and Techniques; Therapeutic Rationale and Termination.

I. Theoretical Considerations

FREUD'S INTERPRETATION OF DREAMS PROVIDED the cornerstone for the psychoanalytic tradition's enduring interest in the classic psychological functions of human life—memory, attention, perception, affect, thought. However, unlike the experimental and academic approach of the classical psychologists, the psychoanalytic tradition studied these phenomena in situ. Not only did this bring "life" into the rather dry and disembodied "mechanisms" of classical psychology, but it brought psychoanalysis together with disciplines that had been developing separately and in relative ignorance of each other, such as anthropology, psychology, history, esthetics. However, the results of these "marriages" have not always been one of equality. Usually psychoanalysts have seen their task to be one of explaining the phenomena of the other disciplines, and less often have they pursued the goal of being informed by them.

Two exceptions come to mind—David Rapaport and Ernest Schachtel. In each, a central concern with affect, attention, memory and thought, combined with primary grounding in the perceptual-expressive investigation into personality (projective testing), led to a wide-ranging attempt to understand human development within a psychological as well as psychoanalytic framework. Other similarities between these two writers also exist; one such example is their view that affect does not only arise as a result of drive-action inhibition or thwarting, a position not often shared by other psychologists and psychoanalysts.1, 2

Ernest Schachtel  

AN EXAMINATION OF THE SELF-IMAGE of the psychodiagnostician has to take into account the conscious and the unconscious ideas and feelings which we have about our professional activity, and requires an attempt to appraise realistically what we are doing and what we should be doing in our work. Reflecting on one's activity in this way can only be salutary and I want to express my appreciation to Dr. Rosenwald for having conceived and planned this symposium. It has been useful to me and I hope it will be of some use to all of us to review and try to clarify some of the many problems revealed by such a self-examination.

Regarding my particular topic (On Self-Doubt and Self-Esteem in the Practice of Psychodiagnostics) it soon became clear to me—and should have been clear when, rather rashly, I chose this topic—that it touches upon the whole range of human motivations and conflicts, on the many sociological factors involved in the various institutional settings and interpersonal relations in which psychodiagnosticians work, and on the historical situation of psychiatry, psychology and psychotherapy. It would be impossible to review all these factors in the time at my disposal. Fortunately, some of them have been discussed and clarified in the section on "The Dynamics of Testing." Others will be taken up by my colleagues in this symposium. I think therefore that it will be more practical and useful if I limit my remarks to two relevant points, namely 1) the problem of alienation of the psychodiagnostician from his work, and, if time permits, 2) an attempt to explore the changing and insufficiently clarified relation of diagnosis to therapy in the fields of psychotherapy and psychodiagnostics. The Consequences of Predicting Disaster11

John Schimel M.D.

John Schimel

John L. Schimel, M.D.
40 Gramercy Park North
New York, New York, 10010

John Schimel  

THE HUMAN IS BORN with very few fears. A catastrophic or shock response occurs when he is in a free fall, has his breath cut off or is exposed to a sudden sharp noise. He will cry when hungry, cold or in pain. He is a long way from panic over crime in the streets, carcinogens in food and in the air we breathe, the threat of unionism, communism, feminism, Zionism, or any other ism, the end of American civilization, the possibility of nuclear warfare, the decline of morality, or the host of other disaster we are promised every day. Erich Fromm once insisted that no sane person could sleep soundly at night because he should be worrying about the possibility of a nuclear holocaust. The journey I wish to trace in this presentation is the one the healthy infant traverses until he becomes Fromm's sane insomniac. Fromm is not alone in being a distinguished and thoughtful authority heavily engaged in admonishing us to worry about impending disaster.

It all begins humbly enough with an infant equipped with a limited (but infinitely expandable) repertory of fears in contact with one or more persons entrusted to preserve him from harm. This all proceeds reasonably well in most instances until the infant becomes ambulatory. Even in the crawling stage, the infant can propel himself swiftly into the proximity of hot radiators, electrical outlets, stairs, the dust behind the sofas, even household poisons in the form of detergents, soap powders and others. In a word, disasters loom on every hand, and the infant must be secured from them. How is this remarkable feat accomplished, so routinely in most cases? And even later, when his ability to walk will expose him to new dangers?

THIRTY-FIVE YEARS AGO the first of Ernest Schachtel's articles on the Rorschach appeared in Psychiatry. It is almost 20 years since Metamorphosis(1959) was first published and 10 since his Experiential Foundations of Rorschach's Test(1966) brought the successive articles on Rorschach together. This paper is less a reappraisal of the meaning and worth of these writings than an account of the continuous use I have made of them as a teacher of graduate students. I have worked with graduate students in psychology, particularly in diagnostic practicums and also have been teaching child development in teacher education graduate school.

It is a somewhat different world today from when we first read the article on "Dynamic Perception and the Symbolism of Form." It is worthwhile to look at what the student today brings to his reading and what may make him responsive. Zeborah Schachtel  

SINCE ERNST1 HAS DIED, again and again the metaphor the mountain climber has come to mind as expressing how he lived his life. A mountain climber, endlessly experiencing the greatness of each mountain he climbed, its special character and unique qualities, he discovered on foot what its vistas were, savoring and forming deep in his mind and heart each of those discoveries. When he spoke of a mountain he knew, it always was like a richly remembered encounter with a wonderful friend, who never would be completely known, the mystery of something infinite, never finished.

He climbed mountains, though physically he was never vigorous or robust. He was tenacious, determined, highly disciplined—and filled with eagerness, excitement, keen appetite, nervous tension, obsessive worry. The tension, anxiety, anguish were always there, but his spirit and his mind could also soar, lifted by a vista, a creature, a breeze, an idea, to join the universe. He set foot knowing it would be a new adventure, each time, full of risk; what would he come to see, be moved by—what grandeur, awesomeness, vastness, sudden intimacy, helplessness?

He climbed, sometimes, with a guide. Whenever he described any of these guides, he conveyed vividly the man's attitude, demeanor, behavior, with few words but with the quality of inner connectedness. I think the attitude of these guides touched something central in himself. They brought to each climb all their experience, knowledge and sense of the mountain and its terrain, but they were alert and ready to experience it that day, in that moment, as it was, aware of each possibility and its consequences, and ready to act.

JOURNAL ENTRY, JUNE 30, 1970:

First writing since Dr. Schachtel's departure for the summer. Miss him. I feel the need to communicate the experiences which are bringing more and more light to a dark and empty interior. The passing thought which comes and is allowed to disappear loses the significance that speech gives to it; more important, saying it to someone you care for. I am tense as I start to write. It is as if I am talking to Ernest. Sitting with my own thoughts and associations is new, but taking them seriously outside of my time with him feels incredible. Even now it is so clear that the affection and familiarity that I feel have to be cloaked in distance. I am so used to being silent and apart … I have trouble believing how much I miss the experience of his presence.

This was written shortly after Dr. Schachtel left for his summer holiday. It could have been written the day after he died.

I knew Ernest Schachtel only as a therapist. We had no relationship beyond the boundary of the therapy room, where we met at an appointed time for an appointed purpose. Invitations which he extended to visit him on Cape Cod during the summer holiday generated panic in me and were gracelessly ignored. Yet I knew him. I knew him through that unique awareness that comes when people share danger, tragedy, or intense struggle. I knew him as a comrade whose protective shield made it safe and profitable to disappear beneath the veil of sanity where one confronts the hidden horrors, deceptions, confusions and emotional conflicts that rob one of his realness. I knew him through the "therapeutic atmosphere" in which it was safe to be defenseless and feel devoid of definition or meaning beyond my puny narcissism. I knew him because the atmosphere was an extension of him; it was of his creation. I knew him through those reflections of me that came through him.

WE CHERISH ERNEST'S MEMORY for what he conveyed to us.

He was a man of keen insights and of the greatest integrity.

Burdened with a frail constitution, he was forced to deal with aspects of life which, for most of us, never become a problem at all.

He developed a special sensitivity and responsiveness to phenomena we fail, for the most part, to perceive. Thinking and studying were at the very center of his life.

His was a genuinely original mind.

Saddened as we are by his loss, he leaves us enriched by his many contributions.—ANYA GOUREVITCH

SULLIVAN USED THIS TERM not only to describe the activity of a therapist, but also the activity of scientific observers, particularly those researchers in the social sciences of anthropology, social psychology and sociology.

As a therapist the term means that one participates in the patient-therapist communication on the basis of careful observation, not only of the patient, but also of the therapist's own reactions, and of the communications that go on between patient and therapist, verbal and non-verbal.

Participant refers to active responsiveness to and communication with the patient by the therapist. It also refers to observation as an active process on the therapist's part.

Observation means that one's therapeutic interventions are based not on a-priori theory, a procrustean bed into which observations are made to fit, but instead, on here and now observations of the relations of the patients' communications, one to another, of omissions in the patients' stories and memories; and of what is going on in the patient interaction. For example, when the therapist notices whenever he says something, that the patient's reaction is to say "no, that's not it" or the like, he can point this out to the patient.

OUR INTENTION IN WRITING THIS ESSAY is to explore the didactic value of Sullivan's concept of participant-observation.

Sullivan was a pioneer who opened new possibilities for those who were interested in intensive psychotherapy. The concept of participant-observation denoted a break with the traditional view of the psychiatrist being a mere observer of the strange world of the mentally disturbed by stressing the participation of the observer in the operational field. Furthermore, the interpersonal approach makes it clear that the nature of the participation of each member is determined by the nature of interactions and the impact of the participants on each other.

Sullivan went perhaps too far in ascribing to this concept a crucial theoretical significance around which he built his operational, interpersonal theory of psychiatry. The concept of participant observation is neither a theory, nor is it a specific technique. It defines an essential attitude—a skill to be developed and cultivated in order to be proficient as a psychotherapist.

Sullivan wrote in 1949 that: "The expertness of the psychiatrist refers to his skill in participant observation of the unfortunate patterns of his own and the patient's living, in contrast to merely participating in such unfortunate patterns with the patient." (Sullivan; 1949)

One can tell much about the quality and style of a psychotherapist by the amount of care and thought he expends on the more humble and routine details of the patient's life. THE LAST TWO DECADES HAVE BEEN rich in observation and research related to the early years of human development. Ethologists, developmental psychologists, and psychoanalysts have made numerous attempts to reassess their own theories with new facts. They have sought to modify and refine explanations which, by necessity, had been limited by the naturalistic or experimental context of their own fields of interest as shown in the work of Ainsworth (1969), (1972), Bowlby (1969), (1973), Duyckaerts (1974), Gewirtz (1972), Harlow (1965), Spitz (1965). Most of these attempts had been centered on the nature and evolution of object relations and attachment behaviors, as they develop during the first two years of life. After this period, it is still mostly uncharted territory as far as the normal development of attachment is concerned: it is even more so when it comes to the relationship between attachment, object relations and transference as it appears in the course of psychoanalysis. This paper is an attempt to discuss this relationship and its impact on the therapeutic management of disturbed adolescents.

EMERGENCIES AND CRISIS ARE ALARMING events which occur within the framework of societal, familial and individual settings. Under ordinary circumstances, there is no particular need to draw a sharp line of distinction between the two concepts.

In intensive psychotherapy, however, crisis and emergency may be considered as two separate events with different connotations and different consequences. It will be shown that there is distinct merit in conceiving of a clinical line of demarcation between the above mentioned phenomena despite their more or less identical overt appearance.

In my definition, an emergency is the occurrence of an urgent situation demanding action. The nature of most emergencies is such that life can go on as usual after the emergency has passed. There is, for all practical purposes, hardly a limit as to the number of times that an emergency can repeat itself without necessarily bringing about a significant change in the person's life style.

In contrast to an emergency, a crisis tends to preclude the possibility of life going on as usual. By definition, crisis is considered to be a decisive or vitally important stage in an individual's existence. It is the point in time when a person comes to a distinct crossroad where he may have to turn in one direction or another without the opportunity of reverting to an old pattern.

ZINBERG AND THE BORISES are to be congratulated for their finely honed work on group process, inspired by Bion, the psychoanalyst who has had such a profound influence at the Tavistock Institute in London, and the A.K. Bion noticed early in his career, while in military service, that regardless of the task that groups of people undertook as a group there were roughly three basic assumption tendencies that interfered with the effectiveness of the group in collaborating towards the accomplishment of that task: namely, a tendency toward dependency in which the group assumes there is something outside of what it does that it must relate to in order to gain the kind of security an immature organism, such as an infant or child, requires; also a tendency to fight or flight assuming that the preservation of the group requires it to be led by the leader or a member towards fighting something or someone or fleeing from something or someone within or outside of the group itself. A YOUNG DOCTORAL STUDENT WHO was writing his thesis on Participant Observation learned that I had worked with Sullivan and asked me what I believed the term meant. The first thought that came to mind was of the character in the play who discovered that all his life he had been speaking prose. In a sense, to the student of interpersonal relations, the term is a redundancy. I trust I can clarify this.

Only forty years ago, most analysts thought that instincts acted on people, and were the root of mental pathology. Sullivan believed it was people acting on people that induced anxiety, and then elucidated the roles of 'significant others' in the development of the individual from infancy on. He studied his own role as psychiatrist in communicating with others, and his observations led naturally to the concept of the analyst as a 'significant other' who not only observed but participated. To him, personality handicaps were due to the presence of anxiety and the lacks in experience. The results of his work with schizophrenics and obsessional compulsives were impressive, and furnished clinical proof of his theory of anxiety, with the therapist as a 'significant other'. The kind of person he was, how and when and what he said and did, were directly related to favorable outcome in treatment and living.

The preponderant view at that time saw the therapist as a pure observer, or 'blank screen', and the patient as the one who 'free associates'. The therapist would make himself as anonymous as possible, remaining removed, distant and detached, at least in theory, lest he influence these free associations. Sullivan, who perceived the situation as an interpersonal field, would say that this orthodox posture was a particular way of participating in a relationship that would have its own effect on what transpired. Thus, no matter that the therapist saw himself as pure observer, he was always a participant in a relationship, for better or worse. This was the nature of things. In essence Sullivan was stating the Heisenberg principle as it operated in human living: the observer is always influencing what he observes.

ERNEST SCHACHTEL'S presence remains that of a tender poetic man, and a keenly reasoning, observant psychoanalyst, rich with the cultural heritage of the European humanists who fled the rising Hitlerism of the 1930's. For me the qualities of this man are epitomized with rare beauty in his article, On Memory and Childhood Amnesia(1947).1

Written 25 years later, a book, Sorrow Beyond Dreams, recently presented as a play on the New York theater scene, by a young Austrian born in 1942 in the thick of the era of the holocaust, somehow evokes for me Ernst's2 presence, in the kind of experience that could be shared with excitment during an evening with Ernst and Zebbie. I would have said something like this:

Here is a gift to us of an existential experience that captures truth better than many of our professional efforts at "case reports" (nor do many would-be "creative" writers succeed). This book, 70 pages of lean and intense writing, draws one into the nonsentimental struggle with the anguish of a son, 30 years old, making the passage of the mourning process involving his mother's suicide. It is a creative process that would do honor to psychoanalysis.

The book moves on two tracks that meet and separate: the line of her life that culminates in its logic of suicide, and his sympathetic fusion and separation from her in her implacable progression.

SUMMARY

Participant observation is a milestone in transcending the original construct of the mirror analyst and the illusion of therapeutic neutrality. Nevertheless, the model has some drawbacks that also deserve to be mentioned. The principle of participant observation contains an element of tautology since all observation includes the observer in what he observes. Every act of observation brings about a modification in the object of the observation. Furthermore, we must appreciate the fact that participant observation is largely based on the element of consensual validation i.e., a system of checking and verification that can in some instances lead to a folie a deux between analyst and analysand. There are a number of rational and irrational components that emerge in the therapeutic alliance. One particular problem centers around the analyst's ability to cope with parataxic phenomena.

It may be useful to view participant observation as a fundamental breakthrough in defining aspects of the analyst's part in the psychoanalytic process. It does not matter that the model has some limitations as long as it is considered to be a viable stepping stone in transcending many aspects of prevailing analytic mystique.

Great care must be taken not to sloganize the term lest the term deteriorate into a verbalism unrelated to constructive, clinical practice. The participant observer cannot be merely an instrumentality that is in tune with epistemological considerations. The model thus defined must make allowance for individual, specifically human attributes of both the observer and the observed. More reliable methods of checking and verification would be useful together with clinically appropriate redefinitions of the transference-countertransference continuum.

PSYCHOANALYSIS IS FUNDAMENTALLY SOUND at the empirical and systematic foundations.1 There, it can be shown, nothing is so intrinsically wrong, deficient, or beyond intelligibility, that continued empirical and systematic inquiry cannot correct for it during the study of the concrete, individual case. The existence of this capacity is, at present, warranted beyond question.

For psychoanalysis, as a coordinated structure of inquiry, is capable, first, of observing and defining, and then, of transforming and explaining, processes and patterns that relate the ongoing, conscious surface to the downgoing, unconscious ground of the experience of any two particular coparticipants. It is, as a direct result, fully capable of being used to explore and to work through the disturbed, distortive, and interlocking relations of that actual, therapeutic experience.

As an experience of therapy undergone, moreover, its focus of inquiry unfolds at the growing edge of processes and patterns that shape the working context for a long-term, intensive, deeply coparticipant effort. Both the psychoanalytic inquiry and the psychoanalytic experience do not, therefore, lack the psychic realism of those uniquely individual, intimately shareable processes and patterns.

SULLIVAN WROTE LITTLE ABOUT his technique as such, focusing instead on the principles and assumptions underlying the words and gestures of the therapist as participant-observer. In 1924 he was already noticing how the "warps" of the psychiatrist affected the psychopathology exhibited by the patient during that session. Henceforth, in all his teaching and writing, he assumed that the psychiatrist is inextricably and inescapably involved with all that is going on in the session. His emphasis, in contrast to most others of his time, was not on eliciting hidden psychopathology, nor upon encouraging a dependent relationship for the uncovering of unconscious fantasies. He explicitly states that clear communication is what he is after. To the extent that a person can clearly articulate and communicate what he is thinking or suffering or whatever-he has a grasp on it. Sullivan stated succinctly, "and no one has grave difficulties in living if he has a very good grasp on what is happening to him."

The notion of participant observation as Sullivan refers to it again and again is as follows: The psychiatrist as a well trained expert, is knowledgeable, about the various fictions or dead weight past figures operating in his present perceptions of other people, so that regardless of how crippled he may be in other human relationships, he nonetheless functions as an effective, skilled participant-observer in enhancing the clarity of the patient's formulation in communication of whatever is ailing him. To do this he must avoid arousing unnecessary anxiety, and must produce some communication before termination of the session that will be beneficial or useful to the patient.

It has always impressed me how much Sullivan emphasizes that in the first interview especially, two strangers are meeting. The patient, regardless of what diagnostic label he has been referred with, is a complete stranger, and hence due all the courtesy, hospitality, and caution due a strange person making one's acquaintance for the first time.

Introduction

TRANSCULTURAL PSYCHIATRIC RESEARCH has sought to determine the influence of social structure and socialization practices of the etiology and symptomatology of personality disorders and to establish general principles which might assist psychotherapists in their efforts to better understand and more successfully treat people from divergent sociocultural backgrounds. Such research has become world wide in its scope and its latest efforts can be assessed from perusal of Transcultural Psychiatric Research Review, now in its thirteenth volume. Recent unpublished studies of the psychological illnesses of immigrants into the United States of members of lower socioeconomic groups have indicated that their form and dynamics can best be understood in terms of the folklore of their native lands. Jerome Singer  

THE DEATH OF ERNEST G. SCHACHTEL was a severe blow to the many people whose lives had touched his directly, and who had benefited from his shy warmth, sensitivity and wisdom. For others who had not had the opportunity to know him personally, his passing represents a setback for the scientific progress of psychoanalysis. Schachtel had undertaken the risky but much needed task of examining the fundamental concepts needed to humanize the overly biologized, outmoded theory that was Freud's legacy. He was trying in his own quiet and deeply thoughtful way to find a metaphor or a scientific image that could preserve the value of the great clinical observations of psychoanalysis, and somehow bring its theory in closer touch with how humans think, feel and talk. In his articles and books, published over several decades, he addressed again and again the question of how we develop a set of basic assumptions that can help us grasp more fully the special humanity of the individual. If a single book can be said to make a difference in lives his great Metamorphosis(1959) can be appraised as that one. Rarely in art or science have wisdom and beauty of language come together so well in one work.

The task that Schachtel set for himself was no less than the formulation of a fundamental psychological model for the interpersonal theory of Sullivan, Fromm, Horney, and various clinicians who adhere to some phase of the increasingly convergent neo-Freudian and existential positions in contemporary psychiatry and clinical psychology. As one delves deeper into the crucial issues of a clinical theory, one is confronted with the necessity for a more precise statement of its underlying premises.

IN JANUARY, 1973 THE SUPREME COURT ruled, by a seven-to-two vote, to legalize abortion in the United States during the first three months of pregnancy. In so doing, it left the choice of abortion a matter for the pregnant woman and her conscience. A New York Times editorial on the decision reminds us that "the Court has performed a useful historical function by recalling that the spur for the initial adoption of state laws banning abortion nearly a century ago was the great risk of maternal death involved in the surgical procedures then used. Now the risk arises out of perpetuating such archaic statutory prohibitions. The effect of these laws has been to force women, especially the young and the poor, to resort to abortion mills instead of expert hospital care when they are determined not to have an unwanted child."

Two and a half years before the Supreme Court ruling, in July 1970, the New York State Legislature passed the nation's first law allowing abortion up to 24 weeks of pregnancy. Free-standing clinics were licensed to perform early abortions and as many as 3, 000 were done in a month at one of the busiest facilities. Women poured in from every part of the United States paying about $150 for the service. As consultant to this clinic I was impressed with the physical and psychological supervision the women received. Abortion counseling was offered to each patient to determine if her decision to terminate her pregnancy was firm. The counselors then followed the patients through the various medical procedures, offering them whatever psychological support seemed necessary. On the day of the abortion the thrust was to allay anxiety.

DR. FEINER'S ZESTFUL retrieval of Freud's "yeastiness" underlines with precision Freud's concern with the toxic effects of analysis on the analyst. Freud's advice to submit to analysis periodically suggests that analysts could contain and accumulate the daily toxic material that emanates from patients' projections for periods of five years or so. More recent technical developments suggest, however, that on-going self-analysis of the countertransference makes it possible for the analyst to cleanse himself as he becomes contaminated by these projections. The old joke about the weary, battleworn young analyst who encounters the older, but fresh and energetic analyst at the end of a long working day and asks him for his secret, and gets the classical reply "But who listens?" should be changed. The older, more experienced analyst might respond: "I also listen to myself."

Dr. Feiner's analysis of the first clinical vignette goes to the core of a complex issue. I agree that the patient "correctly" dismissed an analyst that acted out his counter-transference.

WHY DO PHOBIAS MAKE THEIR FIRST appearance after each of life's two major growth cycles (and why is this association unfamiliar to us)? Early childhood and young adulthood, the two most usual times of onset for phobic symptomatology (Fenichel, 1945) ; (Marks & Gelder, 1966, 1966); (Marks, 1970) ; (Terhune, 1969) are the periods following each of life's two most profound growth surges, the fetal-infancy cycle and the puberty-adolescence cycle (Stuart & Stevenson, 1954). The search for a correlation between growth or growing up as a phenomenon in and of itself (accelerated, as with a major growth cycle, or not) and the appearance of a psychiatric symptom becomes complicated by a psychoanalytic frame of reference and language that unfocuses our thinking away from the forward thrust to human energy and psychic force more than drawing our attention toward it. SUMMARY

I have discussed the psychoanalytic treatment of some psychotic patients in terms of the impact their delusional material had upon me.

I focused on the oppressive nature of the patient's delusion and found that the analyst's reaction with a delusion of his own, so to speak, creates special problems which interfere with the progress of analysis. I described an especially poignant episode where the patient helped me to continue functioning as an analyst.

By contrast, I described another episode which I believe is fairly common and potentially quite disruptive to treatment. In this situation, a patient demanded that I participate in his delusion, that is, intercede for him in the external world. This patient, as did the first patient, also threatened the analytic stance. For analysis to continue it became necessary to demand that the patient maintain an analytic decorum and permit the analyst to analyze rather than participate. The first patient brought a pervasive delusion into the analysis whereas the second patient attempted to bring delusion and the analyst into the external world.

In conclusion, the treatment of psychotic patients does not depend so much upon the content of the patient's psychopathology as it does upon the analyst's sensitivities, sensitivities that are, perhaps, shared by a majority of analysts. The awareness of our sensitivities, usually referred to as countertransference reactions, can only lead to increased integration and forebearance for the analyst. In turn, the range of patients whom we can treat is broadened and the benefits of analysis will become available to a larger number of persons who have, for the most part, known only suffering and misery.

Introduction

FREUD (1905) STATED THAT ONE of the most significant, but also painful psychic achievements of adolescence was the detachment from parental authority. This detachment serves two functions: it allows for and is part of the repudiation of incestuous fantasies; and it permits the development of a new generation with new ideas, and thus furthers civilization. Further, it has an evolutionary function, insofar as it prohibits inbreeding, which would eventually destroy the human race. While Freud did not expand or explain what made the separation so difficult and painful for the adolescent, one factor must certainly be the extended period of dependency of the individual on the family, particularly in our society, where the dependency in childhood and adolescence is enforced by social, economic and educational reasons. This transition from childhood dependency to adult identity often contains one of the central conflicts in adolescence.

This paper will explore some of the ways in which this transition occurs and examine the similarities of the work of Mahler, et al.(1975) on separation-individuation in early childhood, with Erikson's work (1968) on identity crisis and formation in adolescence.6

The structural and dynamic aspects of adolescent individuation and identity formation have been dealt with extensively by both Blos (1962), (1967) and Jacobson (1964), and will not be reviewed here.

IN THE PAST MANY WOMEN came for psychoanalytic treatment for sexual inhibitions such as frigidity. Today, many more come because of guilt and conflict about extra-marital affairs and the feeling of being trapped in marriage. Active, lively, professional women find themselves caught between the divergent requirements of an interesting job and the needs of either husband and family or some less defined need for reaffirmation as a female. The friction between the two parts of her life often makes for interpersonal tensions with husband or partner, and the resulting dissatisfactions or lack of equilibrium may propel her to search for another man or men to satisfy unfulfilled needs. Thus such women lead "double lives" on two levels, professional versus personal and husband versus lover. Moreover, I do not think that the overlap is accidental or unrelated. The common denominator is that these women have an unusual degree of zest, intelligence, competence, and a desire for self-assertion, which makes them unable to "settle" for a safe but often "dull" marriage. They are less likely than average to submit to woman's former fate, to accept that "woman's place is in the home." (Janeway, 1971). However, crippling self doubt may interfere with success.

Years ago it was said that active, lively men needed both a wife and a mistress to complete their lives: one for stability and comfort at home; the other for sexual variety and excitement. Companionship could be gotten with either wife or mistress. The husband might share a great deal about the home and children with his wife, and have a mistress who worked in his professional world and who could share this set of interests with him. His wife might be either indifferent to or jealous of this outer world where she felt excluded.

Ernest G. Schachtel 1903-1975

Earl Witenberg M.D.

Earl Witenberg

Earl Witenberg, M.D., Director
William Alanson White Institute

Earl Witenberg  

FOR THREE DECADES AND MORE have the lifelines of Ernest Schachtel and those of the White Institute been intertwined. He joined the ranks of Erich Fromm, Edith Alt, and Harry Bone as the first non-M.D. members of the Council of Fellows. He faithfully attended all the meetings until failing health prevented his presence. His contributions were quietly effective. His comments were characterized by a quality of allocentric attention. He never lost sight of the basic issues. His appeal was always to the higher sense of the issue. There was a quality of selflessness in his remarks. Nobody will be able to say Ernest was self-seeking. Everyone who attended those meetings can attest his dispassionate, compassionate, principled, and profound interest in furthering the long-range goals of the Institute.

Well-known throughout the community as a teacher, he nevertheless continued to give courses here regularly at a financial sacrifice. He originally gave a course in the Rorschach which was well-attended and profitable for all. In the last 15 years or so he gave case seminars. There his profound knowledge of the human being was communicated to a generation of analysts, and his work lives in their work. Widely sought as training analyst and supervisory analyst, he communicated his human qualities and his professional skills to many. Typical of him, he would prepare for training committee meetings by spending long hours, poring over the records to present with impeccable impartiality the written record of the student under consideration. He has left the Institute the legacy of his scholarly productions as a model.

But, in addition, we will always remember this modest, unassuming man with his dedication to clarity of intellect and affect, decency, his quiet sense of humor, his concern and his sense of dignity. We shall miss him.

Lawrence Epstein  

ISSACHAROFF (1976) HAS STATED THAT IN the 1950's an interest in countertransference emerged with great vigor throughout the world, citing Racker (1948) in Argentina, Winnicott (1949) and P. Heimann (1950) in England, and in this country, Frieda Fromm-Reichmann (1950), Karen Horney (1939), Clara Thompson (1952), Tauber (1952), (1954), and Growley (1952). Most importantly, all of these analysts turned to countertransference to seek a better understanding of the patient in the ongoing process of psychoanalysis. Some went much farther than understanding the patient, but also scrutinized countertransference as a basis for deriving interventions which would facilitate the therapeutic process. I am referring specifically to Racker (1968), Heimann, Winnicott and Tauber, Margaret Little (1957) and Mabel Blake Cohen (1952).

Yet interest in countertransference phenomena did not spread throughout the various psychoanalytic communities at that time. However, it is true that during the past five years, in all schools of psychoanalysis, a wave of interest in countertransference as a valuable component in psychoanalytic psychotherapy, individual and group, has been rising with increasing spirit and vitality. The journals abound in papers on the subject.

This raises two questions. What did delay the scientific study of countertransference? And why have we become so interested in it today?

Why was a widespread interest in countertransference not generated in the 1950's when those remarkable papers were published? Why has it taken so long for us to pay serious attention to it as a therapeutic instrument?

SULLIVAN DEFINED THE PSYCHIATRIC interview as a particular kind of interpersonal relationship which differed from other intimate relationships by its purpose, that "something useful" should be accomplished, namely increased skills of living for one of the people, the patient. Alan Grey  

Chapman, A. H., Harry Stack Sullivan: The Man and His Work New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1976.

THERE ARE THOSE AUTHORITIES WHO claim that Sullivan's ideas have shaped American psychiatry pervasively, but without due recognition. A. H. Chapman is among them. He further asserts that "Some psychiatrists including myself, feel that Sullivan's work makes him the most important figure in psychiatry in the last 100 years, and that his concepts and treatment techniques are much more valid and useful than those of Freud and many others."

These convictions inspired Harry Stack Sullivan: The Man and His Work, Chapman's effort toward a more adequate appreciation of inter-personal theory. The book has several interlocking objectives. Among them, the foremost is to offer an easily readable translation of Sullivan, at a level useful for mental health professionals as well as for intelligent lay people. Another is to illuminate the characteristics of the system through biographical data to suggest how Sullivan's life experiences shaped his insights. Moreover, Chapman intends to provide a balanced assessment of "the weaknesses as well as the strengths of both Sullivan and his work, " instead of falling into that facile and familiar pattern of merely extolling virtues.

A robust affirmation of Sullivan, balanced by the promise of judicious evaluation, evoked very positive anticipations in a fan like me, as I began to read. I mused, it might be just the source to refresh my own memory or to suggest to budding clinicians. The table of contents encouraged these expectations. A first section on "The Life and Emotional Problems of Harry Stack Sullivan" is followed by seven chapters covering his thought.

IT IS OF INTEREST TO SPECULATE about the factors involved in the growing study of the phenomena of countertransference.

As one views society as a whole, one sees increasing openness and candor in all sectors. Concomitant with this mixed blessing, there has been a diminution in the power of authority—whether it be religious or secular, as in the instance of the physician. The breakdown of institutions such as the family, sexual standards, and of government itself has been accompanied by a spate of literature that analyzes authority roles. Once analyzed, they are never the same.

Couple the social pressures ("man is the plaything of social forces defying both his will and his lethargy" [Schwartz, 1976] with the growing maturity of psychoanalysis and you have pressure on the profession to be more open. The widespread acceptance in our field of the fact that each of us can potentially be the other makes us aware of how similar we can be to our patients. We all are more accepting of human frailities than we used to be. It is openly acknowledged that professionals recognize how impossible it is to be a "blank mirror" or be absolutely neutral at all times. With the increasing diversity of the patient population (as indications for psychoanalysis have broadened), has come the realization of the utility of countertransference reactions. The use of face-to-face treatment added to the frequency of countertransference and brought it into fuller use. The seated patient does notice more than the lying one, and does have more of an impact on the analyst.

The following excerpts are taken from Chapter II and Chapter III of my study of countertransference (Wolstein; 1959), 1 and I select them for this symposium, with minor changes, to indicate the general direction of my first working statement that reconceives the early 1950s ego-interpersonal perspective on psychoanalysis along the lines of two-way, coparticipant inquiry by a particular psychoanalyst and his patient into their shared, experiential field of therapy. I select these brief excerpts for consideration here, moreover, because they contain some background references to both Freud's mirror-observational and Sullivan's participant-observational views of that inquiry and experience, and, also, because they present some reasons then set forth that still hold for so reconceiving the structure of psychoanalytic inquiry today (Wolstein, 1977) —by which, empirically, to (1) observe and (2) define the clinical manifestations of, for example, countertransference; then, systematically, to (3) transform and (4) explain them; and, finally, from a pluralism and diversity of speculative perspectives, to (5) interpret them.

For the reader who desires to review the continuity of discussion in the original 1959 context, there is a page citation in parentheses at the end of each excerpt.

DAVID RAPAPORT ENDED HIS book The Structure of Psychoanalytic Theory (1960) with the following statement:

We may not be too far off the mark in suggesting that the malaise of psychology which is manifested in the 'measuring rage' is also responsible for the epidemiclike popularity in psychology of 'information theory, ' 'open systems, ' 'stress syndrome, ' and other imported conceptions. Concepts and methods can be borrowed from other sciences: all that is useful should be used. But grasping at every likely new achievement of other sciences is a giveaway: salvation is expected from the outside and not from results achieved by the sweat of our own brows. At the root of it is a lack of self-confidence: the lack of assurance that psychology knows where it has come from and where it is going.

Alfred Lorenzer did not avoid the sweat of his own brow. He seems to me to be one of the few authors in the field of psychoanalysis who surprises us with fascinating reformulations, insights, and concepts which he develops and explains with the self-confidence of a psychoanalyst who is simultaneously a social scientist.

The task of reviewing his concepts from one book (1973a) is formidable enough, due to the richness of its ideas. In addition, the work of Lorenzer is so intertwined that I must consider other books and publications of his. However, in this paper, I regretfully refrain from discussing the development of his theory of socialization in the broader framework of historical materialism.

OFTEN CRITICIZED FOR HIS CONVOLUTED language and psychiatric neologisms, Sullivan's participant observation and participant observer have become part of the language, filling a need in meaning and, though polysyllabic, seeming apt and comfortable on the tongue. The terms have penetrated the general vocabulary of psychiatry, psychoanalysis and the social sciences. The core of thought unfolds as an axiom of elegant simplicity, with a wide range of implication and application.

In 1939, in his first lecture on Conceptions of Modern Psychiatry, Harry Stack Sullivan referred to participant observation as, "the root premise of psychiatric methodology" (Sullivan, 1940), for the theory which had emerged at the beginning of his career as research psychiatrist. It arose out of thrashing discontent with how psychiatrists were functioning in regard to schizophrenic patients. His compassion for the weak and those all but outcast from the psychiatric world was joined to his search for meaning in their illness and for a foothold for therapy.

And in behalf of these goals, and expressive of his intellectual genius, he, from the beginning of his career, had an overriding interest in forging a scientific methodology for psychotherapy. He drew on ancillary resources via an interdisciplinary approach; another innovation in methodology. Throughout his life his thinking proceeded on two parallel tracks—the humanistic, and the scientific in service to the humanistic.

In a side comment in "The Oral Complex, presented in 1925 at age 32, Sullivan states that for the reconstruction which is needed for the recovery of the schizophrenic, hopefully the therapist can provide "the direct effect of another mind" to neutralize "emotional material of too primitive a nature for any conceptualization in the disordered mind." (Sullivan, 1925).

This description of ideal therapy contrasts to reprimands to therapists as appear in the group of papers which soon followed—and are now published as Schizophrenia as a Human Process (Sullivan, 1962).

THE INDIVIDUAL WAY IN which a person expresses himself in writing may yield valuable information about his personality. First, it may show permanent peculiarities which recur and lend to the written expression a distinctive color which we call the person's " style ". Second, we may detect in single utterances a certain emotion or impulse (the writer may or may not have felt it consciously) which was stimulated by the subject matter and manifests itself through a particular violence of tone, for example, or through slips of the pen, or similar phenomena. A person's style corresponds to his characteristic manner, appearance, bearing, and so forth, while the single utterance corresponds to his behavior in a specific situation. The situation may provoke the discharge of a specific emotion, and the written utterance will be no more than an expression of it, just as oral expression may give vent to an emotion.

That there is some relationship between an individual's personality and the style of his writing, that his style is in some way characteristic of him—this is common knowledge. We can frequently identify an author or a friend through his style.1 But we are interested

L.) attempted in this study to match 630 compositions written by 70 students in order to try to guess which compositions were by each author. While the chance value of correct matchings was 1.6, and the highest possible value (for correct matching) 8, the investigators got a value of 4. The study concerns itself with the degree of identifiability and with the characteristics, on the basis of which one can identify. As such characteristics were regarded: personality traits, content of what was written, value judgment of the investigator on the style (e.g. effective, good, finished, or literary style), form of composition, particular kind of mistakes, and the attitude of the writer toward his writing or the subject of his writing. The authors came to the conclusion that "the precise nature of the characteristic upon the basis of which identification is made, is very elusive" (p.24.), and that it is even "too elusive to be stated adequately in language" (p.69). Martin Kellhacker, in a study "Charakterologische aufsatzuntersuchungen", Zeitschrift für Angewandte Psychologie, vol. 50, pp. 149-182 (1936), in which he does not mention the investigation of Allport and coworkers, describes his attempts to draw conclusions about the personality of the authors of composition (mostly of college freshmen (Oberprima)—. He bases himself mainly on the specific contents of the compositions, and investigates their "language aspect" only in order to discover in what degree the writer has command of the language as a medium of expression, whether language has been an inhibiting or a stimulating factor in his intellectual and total psychic production, in what direction it has tended to carry him away, etc. (p.152)

ERNEST SCHACHTEL CONFRONTS US in his essay (1959) "On Affect, Anxiety, and the Pleasure Principle", with the terms "activityaffect" and "embeddedness-affect", notions which are developed in response to one deterministic Freudian assumption that affect and motoric discharge are mutually exclusive phenomena. Freud (1900), (1911) argues that an infant's restlessness, in the absence of the libidinal object, engenders an increase in drive tension which is measurable as affect; and that, in the presence of the drive object, there is motoric expenditure of instinctual energy, and, hence, no expression of affect. It is with this latter dictum that Schachtel differs. He postulates that affective expression exists in two reduced forms: affects which appear in coordinated, goal-directed actions and embrace, for example, feelings of "eagerness, zest and intentness" (p. 25). These he calls activity-affects. On the other hand, there exist affects arising from wholesale discharge of psychic energy, usually in service to the maintenance (or seeking) of some narcissistically nurtured state. These he terms embeddedness-affects.

Schachtel ultimately sees these affect states as the expressive aspect of personality, organized around active or embedded tendencies, and that the "self-as-organism" has the innate potential toward the pursuit of either developmental line. FROM AMONG SULLIVAN'S MOST IMPORTANT contributions, I want to discuss what seems to me most innovative in his working methods. First, by way of background:

1. Perhaps his fundamental observation was of transference: this did not only develop, he claimed; it was present and ubiquitous from the start. In the language of the English analytic school, introjects and projects are the building blocks of personality and social relations; or as I prefer to say, there are always "other people in the room".

2. These transferences or parataxes are based on experience. Society, not anatomy, is destiny.

3. In dealing with transferences there is no single, detached position from which interventions can be made; the observer is always a participant, reinforcing some projections, diminishing others. Therefore technical activity and flexibility are necessities.

Of course many workers have suggested active and flexible technical measures, perhaps most notably Ferenczi. In our own time, Kernberg has tried to match the difficulties of some transferences with heightened interpretative activity. Kohut has responded with a heightened empathy. Vestiges of Ferenczi's and particularly Alexander's influence continue in the several recommendations for increased manipulations in therapy.
